title: The system said no, twice. He built around it anyway. September 19, 2026.
excerpt: From a blind teenager suing a state board for the right to study physics, to a Bombay lawyer who invented the notation system Indian classical music still runs on, September 19's five stories are about people who refused to accept the rule as written.
bodyHtml:
Most obstacles in these five stories weren't physical - they were rules, written by someone else, that the subject decided didn't have to apply to them. Sometimes that meant a lawsuit. Sometimes it meant inventing an entirely new system from scratch.

A country that only ever imported chips just exported some

Every chip inside an Indian car, phone or inverter used to come from Taiwan, China, or Vietnam. In July 2026, CG Semi's Sanand OSAT facility in Gujarat began commercial production and shipped its first qualified chips to a customer in Japan - Renesas Electronics India. Peak capacity: 300 million units a year, built on a ₹7,600 crore investment across two planned facilities. CG Semi is a joint venture between CG Power (Murugappa Group), Renesas Electronics, and Stars Microelectronics. Before 2024, India assembled essentially zero commercial semiconductors domestically; it now has five units in production.

The board said no. He sued them, and won for every blind student after him.

Srikanth Bolla, blind from birth, topped his Class 10 exams. Andhra Pradesh's state education board told him blind students could only study arts at the intermediate level - not science, not maths. He challenged the rule in court and won, a ruling that applied to every blind student in the state, not just him. He then scored 98%, was admitted to MIT as its first international blind student on full financial aid, and founded Bollant Industries, a packaging manufacturer that deliberately hires people the system had written off.

A lawyer who never performed built the notation Indian music still uses

Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande trained as a lawyer - Elphinstone College, a law degree, practice at the Bombay and Karachi High Courts - before abandoning law for musicology. He classified roughly 180 ragas then in practice into 10 thaats, still the basis of instruction in most Indian music schools, and his six-volume Kramik Pustak Malika recorded over 1,850 compositions using a notation system he invented himself, gathered by travelling India and persuading hereditary musicians to share compositions their families had guarded orally for generations. He'd promised his father he would never perform publicly. He never did, editing his final volumes from his sickbed after a stroke until his death on September 19, 1936.

He started on the bottom rung. He now runs the whole ladder.

Shailesh Jejurikar joined Procter & Gamble in 1989 as an assistant brand manager in India. On July 28, 2025, P&G announced he would become President and CEO effective January 1, 2026 - the first India-born chief executive in the company's roughly 188-year history. He now runs a company with $84.3 billion in annual sales and about 109,000 employees, the maker of Tide, Pampers and Gillette, and in August 2026 was also named Chairman of the Board - both top jobs, 36 years after he started at the bottom of the same company's ladder.

A number nobody had actually counted before

If the global Indian diaspora were counted as its own economy, it would outrank about 170 of the world's roughly 195 countries - not from remittances, but from what it earns. A March 2026 Indiaspora report puts the diaspora's annual earnings from formal employment alone at approximately $730 billion, a figure that excludes business income, stock options and property, meaning the real footprint is larger. Remittances - the number usually reported - are only about 19% of what the diaspora actually earns. An independent economic model from The Australia Today called Indiaspora's figure conservative.

Five stories, one shape: a rule, a ceiling, or an assumption that didn't survive contact with the person it was supposed to constrain. A teenager sued a state board instead of accepting its rule. A lawyer invented a notation system instead of accepting that oral tradition would eventually be lost. A brand manager climbed a corporate ladder nobody expected him to reach the top of. A country stopped only importing and started exporting. And an economic figure that was always true - $730 billion a year - simply hadn't been written down until someone decided to count it.

coverHeadlines: Every chip in an Indian car, phone or inverter used to come from Taiwan, China or Vietnam. In July, a Gujarat plant shipped its first batch out - to a customer in Japan.
A Bombay lawyer never performed music in public. He's the reason Indian classical music has a written notation at all.
A state education board told a blind teenager he couldn't study science. So he sued them - and won.
He started at P&G in 1989 as an assistant brand manager. In January 2026, he became its CEO.
